title: What can your AI see?
bullets: Context that sticks, getting online, connectors
Week 6 · Learn, Vibe, Build · October 5, 2026
notes:
5:05 · 30 seconds

Tonight is mostly live demos, not slides. Three of them. Everything tonight is also one markdown lesson students can paste into their own AI later, so nobody has to catch every word.

(Background for you, not to teach: this whole lecture is the 4D AI Fluency framework in practice. Context files are Description that persists; checking the output out loud is Discernment; deciding what to hand the agent is Delegation; checking before you publish is Diligence.)

title: Tonight: three demos
bullets: 1 · Give your AI context that sticks (AGENTS.md)
2 · Get your project online: a link anyone can open
3 · Connect your AI to the course
notes:
5:05–5:06 · 30 seconds

The through-line, said once: choose what your AI sees, check what it produces, control what it can change. The footer on every slide says which demo we're in.

title: Your AI starts every session from zero
bullets: It only sees what's in front of it right now
It doesn't know your project unless you tell it
A generic answer is usually a context problem
notes:
5:06–5:07 · 1 min

The context window is what the model sees for this answer: your message, the chat so far, files and tool results. Training knowledge is separate; app 'memory' is the app looking things up for it. Ask the room: who has had to re-explain their project to an AI three times this week?

(Background: this is Description. A good description says what you want (product), how to approach it (process) and how to behave (performance).)

title: Markdown: plain text with a little structure
bullets: # Big heading
## Smaller heading
- a bullet point
**bold**  *italic*
[a link](https://example.com)
`some code`
notes:
5:07–5:08 · 1 min

A .md file is just a text file. # makes headings, - makes lists. Humans can read it raw; AIs read it really well. Every lesson on the course site is a markdown file you can copy. You've seen it already: AI chat answers are written in markdown.
extra: Plain text. Readable by you and by your AI.

title: AGENTS.md: context that sticks
bullets: A markdown file in your project folder
Coding agents read it at the start of every session
AGENTS.md: Codex, Cursor, many others · CLAUDE.md: Claude Code
In a chat app: paste it in, or add it to a Project
notes:
5:08–5:09 · 1 min

Write it once and stop re-explaining your project. What goes in: who it's for, what it is, the stack, conventions, where facts live, and what 'done' looks like. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, and also reads AGENTS.md in practice (verified today); a CLAUDE.md that just says 'see AGENTS.md' covers both. Always check the tool actually read it: ask it what the project is.

title: What goes in AGENTS.md
bullets: Who it's for, and what they need
What it is, in one sentence
Stack and conventions ("plain HTML, no build step")
Where the facts live (and "never invent facts")
What "done" looks like
Keep it short, true, and secret-free
notes:
5:08–5:09 · 1 min

Six headings are enough. The most useful line is often a rule: never invent facts, only use docs/event-facts.md. Short beats long: the agent reads all of it every session, so every line should earn its place. Never put passwords or API keys in it; it's a file in your repo.

title: Live demo · the same question, twice
bullets: 1 · Open the project. Ask: “Improve the homepage.”
2 · Write AGENTS.md together (2 min)
3 · Ask again. Compare.
4 · Fresh session: does it still know?
5 · Add an index pointing to docs/
notes:
5:09–5:17 · 8 min LIVE · exact steps and prompts on the demo script page

Repo: github.com/unforcedagi/lvb-week6-demo (Hill Plant Swap, fictional). It has NO AGENTS.md on purpose.
1. (1 min) Open it in your agent. Prompt: 'Improve the homepage.' Expect generic: invented dates, maybe a framework, a 'garden lovers' audience.
2. (3 min) Write AGENTS.md live, asking the room for each line: who it's for, what it is, stack, conventions, facts, what done looks like.
3. (2 min) Same prompt. Narrate what you check: are the facts from docs/event-facts.md? Phone-first? No framework? (That narration is discernment; don't name it.)
4. (1 min) Quit, start a fresh session, ask 'What is this project and who is it for?' It knows: the file persists, the chat didn't.
5. (1 min) Show the 'Where to look' section: the index.
IF IT STALLS: the prepared AGENTS.md is on the demo script page. Paste it, and show the rehearsal output tab. Never show invented output.
extra: Same question. Different context. Different answer.

title: A real AGENTS.md (the demo's)
bullets: # Hill Plant Swap
Who: first-year students on phones, nervous
What: one page announcing a free monthly swap
Stack: plain HTML + CSS, no JavaScript
Facts: only docs/event-facts.md; never invent
Done: date + place readable at 390px in 10 s
notes: Shown after the demo, 30 seconds. This is roughly what we just wrote live. The full template is on the Week 6 page: copy it, fill it in for your own project tonight in studio.
extra: Six lines. Every session starts here.

title: Index files: a map, not a dump
bullets: ## Where to look
- docs/event-facts.md: the only source of facts
- docs/audience.md: who visits
- research/index.md: interview notes (its own index)
notes:
5:17 · 30 seconds (shown at the end of Demo 1)

The demo repo starts with one doc; this is how the index grows. A short top file says what exists and links deeper. The AI reads the small map, then opens only what it needs. Indexes nest: an index can point to other indexes. The course site does exactly this: cu.learnvibe.build/llms.txt is an index of every lesson (live tonight after class).
extra: The AI reads the map, then opens only what it needs.

title: Your link has to work on someone else's phone
bullets: ✗  file:///Users/you/Desktop/project/index.html
only works on your laptop
✓  https://you.github.io/project/
works for anyone, anywhere
notes:
5:17–5:18 · 1 min

This is the most common problem in submissions so far: a link that points to a file on your own computer. If the address starts with file:// or C:\, nobody else can open it. Test: send the link to yourself and open it on your phone, off wifi.
extra: If it starts with file://, nobody else can see it.

title: Three different things
bullets: Git: save points for your project, on your laptop
GitHub: a copy of those save points, online
Pages / Vercel: turns that copy into a website
notes:
5:18–5:19 · 1 min

Commit = a save point with a note. Push = send your save points to GitHub. Deploy = publish. Most confusion comes from treating these as one thing.

title: Live demo · from folder to link
bullets: 1 · Download the project folder
2 · GitHub Desktop: create repo, commit, publish
3 · Settings → Pages → main → Save
4 · Open the link on a phone
5 · Change something, commit, push, refresh
notes:
5:19–5:27 · 8 min LIVE · exact clicks on the demo script page

Use the zip from the class files page so you start from a plain folder with no git history.
1. Unzip. GitHub Desktop: File → Add local repository → choose the folder → 'create a repository' → Create.
2. Commit to main ('first version'). Publish repository; UNTICK 'keep this code private'.
3. On github.com: Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from a branch → main / (root) → Save. About a minute.
4. Open the https://<you>.github.io/<repo>/ link on your phone; hold it up.
5. Ask the agent for one small change, commit, push, refresh after ~1 min.
While Pages builds, say: Vercel does the same for React/Next/Vite projects: import the GitHub repo at vercel.com/new and click Deploy.
IF PAGES IS SLOW: show the already-live copy at unforcedagi.github.io/lvb-week6-demo and move on. The handout 'Get your project online' has every step with a no-install option.
extra: Handout: “Get your project online”, step by step.

title: When the link doesn't work
bullets: 404: wait 1–2 min, then check Settings → Pages
Page with no styles: paths start with / (use style.css)
Only the README shows: index.html must be in the top folder
Old version: hard refresh, or wait a minute
Private repo on a free plan: make it public, or use Vercel
notes: 5:27 · 30 seconds. The handout's fix-it table, in brief. Most first deploys hit one of these. Name them so nobody feels stuck alone; the handout on the Week 6 page has the full steps.

title: API vs. MCP
bullets: API: one service's own menu of requests
MCP: one standard plug for AI apps to use many tools
MCP servers often call APIs underneath
notes:
5:27–5:28 · 1 min

API = how one program asks another for things; every service's menu is different. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard: write the connector once, use it in any MCP-capable app. Analogy: different wall sockets vs a universal adapter. Reading adds context; writing (sending, paying, deleting) changes the world. Start read-only; ask before anything that changes things. A web page that says 'ignore your instructions' is data, not your boss.

title: Live demo · connect your AI to this course
bullets: https://api.learnvibe.build/mcp
Add it as a custom connector (or `claude mcp add`)
Ask: “Using the course connector, teach me tonight's lesson on AGENTS.md, then quiz me.”
notes:
5:28–5:33 · 5 min LIVE

Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http lvb https://api.learnvibe.build/mcp, then start claude and run /mcp to see it connected.
Claude app: Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → paste the URL (plans vary).
Ask it to list the lessons, then to teach the AGENTS.md part and quiz you. It's read-only and public: no student data, nothing it can change. That's the safe way to start with any connector.
IF IT STALLS: open cu.learnvibe.build/lessons/week-6/lesson.md, copy it, paste into any chat with the same prompt. Same result, no connector.

title: Choose · check · control
bullets: Choose what it sees: context files, connectors
Check what it produces: fluent ≠ correct, say what you checked
Control what it can change: read-only first, ask before writes
This course's connector is read-only, on purpose
notes: 5:33 · 30 seconds. The through-line, made concrete. Background (not taught): this is Description, Discernment, Delegation and Diligence in practice. A connector that can write (send email, edit files) deserves a pause: what can it change, and can you undo it? Content an AI reads can contain instructions (prompt injection); treat it as data.

title: This week's reading: your AI as a coach
bullets: Arielle Shipper, “How to Get Better at AI by Asking AI” (Every)
Ask your AI: which of the eight levels am I, with examples?
Then: “teach me the next step”
notes:
5:33–5:35 · 2 min

Shipper asked her AI to place her on Every's Eight Levels of AI Adoption from her actual past work, turned that into recommendations, then had it teach her the next step. Same move as tonight: give your AI context about you, and it can coach you. Free plan or no chat history? Paste your AGENTS.md or your last two submissions and ask 'what level am I, with examples?' Gift link: on your account page and in tonight's announcement. No due date.
Then: trios, 5:35–6:05.

title: Studio · write each other's AGENTS.md
bullets: Pairs, 20 minutes
8 min each: your partner interviews you and drafts your AGENTS.md
4 min: test it with your own agent, then revise
notes:
6:05–6:25 · 20 min PAIR ACTIVITY (show at 6:05, after trios)

Interview questions: Who is this for? What is it, in one sentence? What's it built with? What should the AI never do? Where do the facts live? What does done look like? Partner types; owner corrects. Then each person opens their own project, adds the file, asks their agent 'What is this project and who is it for?' and one real task, and revises what it got wrong. No project yet? Write it for the project you want to start. Then 6:25–6:55: build with it, and get it online (use the handout).
